name: Headphone power
seoDesc: Headphone power: work out voltage (RMS) from the impedance and the DBSPL @ 1 V RMS. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: voltage (RMS) is what the Headphone power calculator works out, and it gets there from the impedance, the DBSPL @ 1 V RMS and the loudness. That makes it useful for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Headphone power calculator work?
sections.html:
The Headphone power calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports voltage (RMS) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the impedance (R), the DBSPL @ 1 V RMS and the loudness (dBSPL).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in ohms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in dBSPL.
  • A number, expressed in dBSPL.

sections.title: The formula behind the Headphone power calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Voltage (RMS)=((1 ÷ 100) × the square root of (10) × the square root of (impedance (R) × ((10, -1 ÷ 10 × DBSPL @ 1 mW + (1 ÷ 10) × loudness (dBSPL)))))
Power (average)=((10, -1 ÷ 10 × DBSPL @ 1 mW + (1 ÷ 10) × loudness (dBSPL)))
DBSPL @ 1 mW=DBSPL @ 1 V RMS + 10 × ((1 ÷ 1000) × impedance (R))
Current (RMS)=(((1 ÷ 100) × the square root of (10) × the square root of (impedance (R) × ((10, -1 ÷ 10 × DBSPL @ 1 mW + (1 ÷ 10) × loudness (dBSPL))))) ÷ impedance (R))
Amp impedance should be less than=((1 ÷ 8) × impedance (R))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Impedance (R) = 10 Ω and Loudness (dBSPL) = 10. The calculator returns Amp impedance should be less than = 1 Ω.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Amp impedance should be less than = 1 Ω should be roughly the size you expected from Impedance (R) = 10 Ω and Loudness (dBSPL) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in volts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in milliwatts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in milliamperes, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.
  • Shown in ohms, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Power, opening in milliwatts
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in milliamperes
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Headphone power calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the impedance, the DBSPL @ 1 V RMS and the loudness — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Headphone power calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns voltage (RMS), derived from the impedance, the DBSPL @ 1 V RMS and the loudness. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Headphone power calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the impedance, the DBSPL @ 1 V RMS and the loudness, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter impedance (R) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Impedance (R) opens in ohms and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Amp impedance should be less than = 1 Ω. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Headphone power calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
